Twenty tritone reproductions of portraits made between 1972–1985. Hardcover, 10.5 × 11 inches (26.7 × 27.9 cm), 56 pages. ISBN 9783958291065. Out of print. Cover portrait of Susan Sontag, 1975.

title: Twentysix Luxury Brands
description: Twentysix Luxury Brands is a photographic zine by MarieVic, shot in New York City during election week 2020 as the country's high-end shopping districts boarded up their storefronts in anticipation of post-election unrest. Plywood window coverings blanket the strip whose extroverted glassed windows are normally meant to speak a language of enticement instead, the brands appear behind raw plywood, unbranded for a week, identifiable only by location and embossed nameplates. The book takes its title and structure from Ed Ruscha's 1963 artist book Twentysix Gasoline Stations, the foundational gesture of conceptual photobook practice that traded fine-art subjects for the deadpan repetition of the American landscape. MarieVic joins a long lineage of Ruscha homages—Mishka Henner's Eighteen Swimming Pools, Jeff Brouws's Twenty-four Former Filling Stations, and others—that adopt the "number-subject-location" formula and Ruscha's clinical typography to address consumerism, urban decay, and the passage of time. Here the formula meets a specific moment in 2020 New York, in which the architecture of luxury was briefly and bluntly remade as defensive infrastructure.
tags: Photography, Zine, MarieVic, New York City, 2020 Election, Storefronts, Boarded Up, Luxury, Conceptual Photography, Ruscha Homage, Blurring Books, Artist Book
notes: Self-published by MarieVic via her Blurring Books imprint, 2020. Title and structure are a deliberate homage to Ed Ruscha's Twentysix Gasoline Stations (1963) — part of the long Ruscha-tribute lineage that includes Mishka Henner's Eighteen Swimming Pools and Jeff Brouws's Twenty-four Former Filling Stations. 60 pages, 6 × 10 inches, softcover. title: There Is No Light at the End of the Tunnel Because the Tunnel Is Made of Light
description: Ryan Spencer's There Is No Light at the End of the Tunnel Because the Tunnel Is Made of Light is a 272-page paperback that imagines the visual companion to a film that was never made: the unrealized cinematic version of The Afghan Whigs' 1996 album Black Love. Spencer assembles film stills culled from the deep catalogue of neo-noir Los Angeles cinema and arranges them so that the album's track titles and song-by-song narrative drive the sequence, making a found-image storyboard for a record that always wanted to be a movie. The accompanying fictional essay by Rebecca Bengal extends the conceit into prose Chummy Alexanian's illustrations punctuate the book with hand-drawn motifs that play against the cinematic source material. Published in TBW Books' small-format paperback line with colored edges, the volume sits between artist book, music object, and pulp paperback — a physical artifact whose stylized object qualities are integral to its meaning. The result is at once a tribute to Greg Dulli's record, an essay on appropriation and cinephilia, and a meditation on the gap between what an album promises and what a film could have delivered.

title: FLOWERS
description: FLOWERS is a collaborative artist book by Kenta Cobayashi and Tyrone Williams, published by Photobook Daydream Editions in a first edition of 100. The work pairs the two photographers' practices through a shared image-language built at the seam where photographic capture meets generative AI: source photographs of flowers and floral arrangements are fed through the artists' respective digital processes, then iteratively transformed—first by the artists themselves, then extended further into computational realms—until the resulting images sit between document, painting, and rendered object. The collaboration is in keeping with both photographers' wider concerns: Cobayashi (b. 1992, based in Tokyo) is known for warped, post-photographic image-making that pushes against the boundary between photograph and digital artifact, while Williams (based in New York) develops image work that interrogates surface, code, and abstraction. As a small softcover edition of 100, FLOWERS reads as a discrete proposition rather than a survey—a 64-page experiment in what intentional collaboration with AI tools looks like for two artists already working at the edges of computational photography.

title: Passports
description: Passports is Keisha Scarville's first major monograph, anchored on more than three hundred reinterpretations the artist has made of her father's passport photograph. Working over the original picture with paint, beads, gold leaf, glitter, and fragments of other Black bodies, Scarville turns a state-issued document of identification into a serial portrait practice — at once a private memorial and a public meditation on how citizenship, personhood, and Black diaspora are inscribed in and resisted by the bureaucratic image. The reworked passports are interleaved with archival photographs from her father's life in Guyana and New York between the 1960s and 1980s, his self-portraits, Scarville's own landscape photography, and transcripts of conversations with him before and after his death. A new essay by Tina M. Campt — Professor of Humanities at Princeton and a leading voice on the visual culture of Black diaspora — situates the project alongside Campt's own thinking on listening to images and the quiet frequencies of Black archives. Published by MACK in May 2026 in a 280-page debossed Swiss hardcover, the volume is at once a daughter's elegy and a sustained argument that the archive is something we make, not something we receive.

title: Richard Prince
contributors: Ralph Gleis (Foreword), Christian Liclair, Walter Moser, Nicole Scheyerer, Eva Kernbauer, Sydney Stutterheim, Thomas D. Trummer
description: A retrospective catalog accompanying Richard Prince's major Albertina Museum survey (Vienna, on view through 16 August 2026), curated by Walter Moser. The volume gathers approximately 150 works spanning Prince's practice from the 1970s to the present and presents his photographic work alongside forays into installation, drawing, painting, and collage. Iconic series — including the Cowboys, the Fashion pieces, and the rephotographed advertising images that established Prince as a central figure of Appropriation Art — appear alongside rarely seen and previously unpublished material. Essays by Christian Liclair, Walter Moser, Nicole Scheyerer, Eva Kernbauer, Sydney Stutterheim, and Thomas D. Trummer address collage and montage technique, mythical masculinity, spiritual imagery, portraiture, and the conceptual stakes of appropriation. A foreword by Ralph Gleis frames the catalog within the Albertina's program. Prince's strategy — removing commercial context from images already saturated by media use, then re-staging them as art — interrogates authorship, originality, and the cultural codes embedded in American consumer imagery. 280 color illustrations.
tags: Art, Photography, Appropriation, Monographs, Retrospective, Cowboys, American Art
notes: Catalog for Richard Prince retrospective at the Albertina Museum, Vienna exhibition on view through 16 August 2026. Approximately 150 works. Distributed in North America by University of Chicago Press for Hirmer Verlag.

title: New Cowboys
description: A limited-edition artist's publication (edition of 500) from Karma continuing Richard Prince's decades-long Cowboys project, in which the artist rephotographs the lone, anonymous, often weathered cowboy figure from cigarette advertisements and other mass-market American sources. This 24-page edition presents a new group of cowboy images that foreground the tears, scratches, and surface textures of Prince's source material — exposing the physical residue of the appropriated print as part of the picture itself. Prince's Cowboys works, begun in 1980, were among the foundational gestures of Appropriation Art and helped reframe rephotography as a critical practice rather than reproduction. Printed at a large 15¼ × 11½-inch trim, the publication functions as both an artist's edition and a distillation of Prince's continued investigation of the cowboy as American myth.

title: Kiss of the Sun
description: A catalogue published on the occasion of Lee Mary Manning's third solo exhibition at CANADA, New York (22 November 2024 – 11 January 2025). The 100-page book features images of framed works from the show alongside collaged photographs and digital scans of ephemera — both objects included in the exhibition and material that did not end up on the wall. Manning's practice moves fluidly between photographic registers — daily diaristic shooting, found-image collage, and the digital flatbed scan — and the catalogue mirrors that working method on the page rather than presenting only the framed end-products. Designed by Joe Gilmore. Published by CANADA, the artist-run gallery at 60 Lispenard Street founded in 1999.

title: Cruising Pavilion: Architecture, Dissident Sex and Cruising Cultures
description: Edited by Pierre-Alexandre Mateos and Charles Teyssou, Cruising Pavilion maps how cruising cultures have shaped architectural and urban environments. The 432-page volume builds a typology of spaces produced by sexual subcultures — parks, restrooms, streets, sex clubs, bathhouses — alongside the virtual geographies that emerged with dating apps. Essays and case studies trace how artistic avant-gardes have worked at the intersection of sex, art, and architecture, following the eponymous curatorial project initiated by Mateos, Rasmus Myrup, Octave Perrault, and Teyssou, which travelled from Paris to Venice, New York, Fire Island, and Stockholm. Designed by Natasha Agapova. Thread-sewn softcover.

description: The fourth volume in Spector's Schools of Departure series examines the use of technology in post-Bauhaus design education. In the second half of the twentieth century, universities and research institutions were swept by a wave of cybernetisation as the triad of knowledge, technology, and progress surfaced again undaunted this book reflects on how designers and architects have conceptualised machines — and their relationship to them — across the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Edited by Regina Bittner, Katja Klaus, and Philipp Sack for the Bauhaus Dessau Foundation. title: (Inter)Faces of Predictions
description: (Inter)Faces of Predictions, a collaboration between writer-researcher Megan Williams (b. 1995, London) and visual artist Sheung Yiu (b. 1991, Hong Kong based in Helsinki), examines how faces are read across cultural and technological contexts to attribute character traits and forecast the future. The project sets East Asian face-analysis traditions and Western physiognomy alongside contemporary facial-recognition technology, with Yiu analysing his own face to show how historical belief systems and modern algorithmic procedures reproduce remarkably similar biases. Archival material, photographic work, and technological methods are woven together to bridge historical discourse and contemporary AI critique. Co-published by Spector Books and the C/O Berlin Foundation in connection with the C/O Berlin Talent Award 2025. 640 pages, thread-bound softcover. Trilingual: English, Chinese, German.

title: IDEA - KUTT Magazine (The Book)
description: A facsimile edition collecting all three issues of KUTT, the cult dyke zine published between 2002-2003 in Amsterdam. Originally conceived as the lesbian counterpart to BUTT Magazine, KUTT was founded by Jessica Gysel, Martien Mulder, and Marjolein Rams. The magazine's signature lilac pages featured it-girl actor Chloë Sevigny, acclaimed writer and activist Eileen Myles, experimental filmmaker K8 Hardy, and feminist queer icon Peaches (Merrill Nisker). Photography by Ryan McGinley, Collier Schorr, Viviane Sassen, and Martien Mulder captured the burgeoning lesbian scene with the same bold spirit and tongue-in-cheek attitude as its sister publication. Despite lasting just three issues, KUTT quickly gained cult status among queer creatives, fashion insiders, and indie mag obsessives. Published by IDEA as a complete facsimile in an edition of 1,000 copies, reproducing the original issues page-for-page.

title: Index #8
description: The eighth issue of e-flux Index, a quarterly print journal surveying contemporary culture through e-flux's publishing on art, theory, architecture, film, criticism, activism, and art education. This 560-page volume explores the fragmentary complexity of the current moment through eleven emergent thematic snapshots drawn from texts commissioned throughout spring 2025. Features 142 contributors including authors, artists, architects, filmmakers, poets, and educators—among them Evan Calder Williams, Fred Scharmen, Chris Murtha, Filipa Ramos, and Rory Rowan. Each issue interweaves long-form essays, exhibition and book reviews, and critical discussions from various e-flux publications. Released January 2026, Index #8 continues e-flux's mission to capture the breadth and depth of contemporary cultural discourse in a substantial print format. Distributed by Antenne Books, Les presses du réel, Asterism Books, Art Metropole, The Book Society, and Buchhandlung Walther König.

title: Brush Fires in the Social Landscape
contributors: Nan Goldin, Karen Finley, Kiki Smith, Vince Aletti, C. Carr, Fran Lebowitz, David Cole
description: A seminal work begun in collaboration with David Wojnarowicz before his death in 1992 from AIDS-related complications. This monograph demonstrates Wojnarowicz's extraordinary use of photography, often done in conjunction with writing or painting, to address the AIDS crisis and issues of censorship and homophobia. The work includes contributions from artist and writer friends including Lucy R. Lippard, Nan Goldin, Karen Finley, Kiki Smith, and others, to David Cole, the lawyer who represented him in his case against Donald Wildmon and the American Family Association. Published as Aperture 137, this book captures Wojnarowicz's fierce engagement with political and social issues through his multimedia artistic practice.

title: Richard Prince: Untitled (couple)
description:
One Work is a unique series of books published by Afterall, with each presenting a single work of art considered in detail by a single author. The primary aim of the series is to provoke debate about significant moments in contemporary art's recent development.

By rephotographing an image from a magazine to make his 1977 work Untitled (couple), Richard Prince extracted the uncanny from the generic, locating the mysterious essence hidden behind the veil of advertisement. Working as a photo archivist at Time Life, Prince conceived his first body of appropriated work in 1977, creating what he would later dub "rephotography"—eliminating all surrounding text and imagery that would contextualize the image as an ad. In the process, Prince updated the readymade for the late 1970s and early 1980s, an age in which the image was the be-all and end-all.

Drawing on an unpublished interview with Richard Prince, Michael Newman analyses this seminal work, connecting it to ideas of allegory, simulacrum, and the formation of personal identity in a society of commodity and spectacle. Newman argues that the vintage TV series The Twilight Zone is crucial to understanding Prince's use of images. During the 1960s, structuralism recast the image as text; Prince's work, Newman argues, revived the image in such a way that it is irreducible to text. The series questions issues of mass consumerism, reality vs. fiction in advertising, and identity formation in a commodity culture.

Richard Prince (b. 1949, Panama Canal Zone) is a member of the Pictures Generation of artists that emerged in the 1980s. His works are held in the collections of The Museum of Modern Art, the Art Institute of Chicago, the Goetz Collection (Munich), and the Victoria and Albert Museum (London).
tags: Art, Photography, Appropriation Art, Contemporary Art, Pictures Generation, Richard Prince, Conceptual Art
notes: Part of Afterall's One Work series examining single works of contemporary art. Newman's analysis draws on unpublished interview with Richard Prince. The 1977 Untitled (couple) series was one of Prince's earliest appropriation works, created while he worked as a photo archivist at Time Life magazine. Prince is considered a founding member of the Pictures Generation.

title: 13 Photographs
description: Published in Hamden, Connecticut by Ives-Sillman in 1978, this is the prospectus booklet for Herbert Matter’s portfolio 13 Photographs, devoted entirely to the sculptor Alberto Giacometti. The thirteen plates comprise a portrait of Giacometti and twelve photographs of his sculpture, drawn from the body of work Matter began in 1960 on his first visit to the artist’s Paris studio. Swiss-born photographer and graphic designer Herbert Matter (1907–1984) met Giacometti through Pierre Matisse in 1950 and was commissioned to photograph and design the Guggenheim’s 1955 Giacometti catalogue. Giacometti was astonished by the resulting images, writing that each was “a creation in itself” and that they revealed aspects of his sculpture he had never seen. The portfolio carries texts by the painter and critic Louis Finkelstein and the photographer Baldwin Lee, who taught alongside Matter at Yale. The publication holds particular significance as the final edition issued by Ives-Sillman, the New Haven imprint of graphic designers Norman Ives and Sewell Sillman, appearing in 1978 shortly after Ives’s death. Matter’s two-decade Giacometti project was ultimately gathered in the monograph Giacometti (Abrams, 1987), completed after his own death in 1984.

notes: Prospectus for the Ives-Sillman portfolio; thirteen images depict a portrait and twelve sculptures of Alberto Giacometti. Ives-Sillman’s final publication, issued 1978 after Norman Ives’s death. Texts by Louis Finkelstein and Baldwin Lee. Sources: J.N. Herlin, Inc.; Guggenheim Museum; Wikipedia.

title: 2000 BC: The Bruce Conner Story Part II
contributors: Kathy Halbreich, Bruce Jenkins, Peter Boswell
description: Published by the Walker Art Center, Minneapolis, to accompany the 1999–2000 retrospective of the same name (Walker Art Center, October 9, 1999 – January 2, 2000, then touring to three further venues), this is the most comprehensive monograph to date on Bruce Conner (1933–2008), one of the most inventive and elusive figures in postwar American art. Across roughly 280 pages it surveys five decades of Conner’s restless, cross-disciplinary practice — assemblage, found-object sculpture, drawing, collage, printmaking, photograms, and the pioneering experimental films (A Movie, Cosmic Ray, Crossroads) that made him a foundational figure in American avant-garde cinema. Edited by Joan Rothfuss, with essays by Walker director Kathy Halbreich and curators Bruce Jenkins and Peter Boswell, and designed by Andrew Blauvelt with Erin Mulcahy, the volume is profusely illustrated with 75 four-color and 175 black-and-white plates and finely printed in Germany by Cantz. Extensive back matter includes an exhibition checklist, chronology, selected bibliography, filmography, and index. The catalogue received second prize in the 1999–2000 International Association of Art Critics (AICA/USA) awards. The playful title nods to Conner’s lifelong resistance to retrospective summary — a sequel to a “Part I” that never existed.

notes: Exhibition catalogue for the Walker Art Center retrospective (Oct 9, 1999 – Jan 2, 2000), which traveled to three further venues. title: Nervous Breakdown
contributors: René Zechlin, Astrid Ihle (foreword); Max Dax, Robert Eikmeyer, Kim Gordon, Ulrich Loock (essays)
description: Subtitled Album Covers, this is the first book to gather every record, CD, and cassette sleeve since 1979 to feature the artwork of Raymond Pettibon (b. 1957), the Southern California artist whose ink drawings became the visual signature of American punk and alternative music. Spanning more than four decades, it traces his collaborations with Black Flag (whose logo and early sleeves he designed for his brother Greg Ginn’s SST label), Sonic Youth, Foo Fighters, Iggy Pop, Minutemen, and, more recently, Lana Del Rey, mapping Pettibon’s outsized influence on the look of alternative culture from the late 1970s to today. Drawn from the Stefan Thull Collection, the volume reproduces 301 illustrations and carries a foreword by René Zechlin and Astrid Ihle and essays by Max Dax, Robert Eikmeyer, the musician and artist Kim Gordon, and Ulrich Loock. Designed by Studio Sven Michel, Berlin, and printed by VeronaLibri, it was published by David Zwirner Books with the Wilhelm-Hack-Museum to accompany the exhibition of more than 200 works from the Thull collection in Ludwigshafen, Germany.

notes: Subtitle: Album Covers. Published with the Wilhelm-Hack-Museum, Ludwigshafen, to accompany an exhibition of 200+ Pettibon-illustrated music sleeves from the Stefan Thull Collection. 301 illustrations; designed by Studio Sven Michel, Berlin; printed by VeronaLibri, Verona. Source: David Zwirner Books.

title: Magnetics
description: A pocket-sized monograph on the Belgian painter Michaël Borremans (b. 1963), among the most admired painters of his generation, whose small, darkly lit canvases fuse the technique of the old masters with the framing of cinema and the displacements of Surrealism. Published by Hatje Cantz for the exhibition Magnetics at BAWAG Contemporary, Vienna, the book presents a concise selection of about a dozen canvases made over the preceding five years, shown alongside related drawings and films. Its sixteen color plates concentrate on the enigmatic, psychologically charged portraits and figure studies for which Borremans is known — faces half-swallowed by shadow, gestures suspended mid-action, meaning withheld. A text by Christine Kintisch situates the work within Borremans’s wider practice. Compact at roughly 11 × 17 cm and 60 pages.
tags: Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, Belgian Art, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Published for the exhibition Magnetics at BAWAG Contemporary, Vienna. 16 color plates; text by Christine Kintisch. Source: David Zwirner / Hatje Cantz.

title: Horse Hunting
description: Published by David Zwirner on the occasion of Michaël Borremans’s second solo exhibition at the gallery (New York, March 7 – April 1, 2006), this hardcover catalogue documents a body of fourteen new paintings, among them the eponymous Horse Hunting (2005) — a portrait of a young, fashionably dressed man holding a twig to each nostril, whose deadpan strangeness is typical of the Belgian painter (b. 1963). Borremans’s pictures pair old-master technique with disquieting, hard-to-place imagery, resisting straightforward narrative or interpretation. Illustrated boards, no dust jacket as issued, with sixteen color reproductions and a text by the Belgian artist and curator Hans van Heirseele. Printed by Earth Enterprise, New York.

notes: Catalogue for Borremans’s second David Zwirner solo show (Mar 7 – Apr 1, 2006), fourteen new paintings including Horse Hunting (2005). Illustrated boards, no dust jacket as issued; 16 color plates; text by Hans van Heirseele; printed by Earth Enterprise, New York. Cover image: OpenLibrary. title: 121 Nurses
description: A layered work of appropriation by the New York conceptual artist Eric Doeringer (b. 1974), best known for the “bootleg” miniatures of blue-chip artworks he sold on the street outside art fairs and for his Copycat Publications, which meticulously re-create rare conceptual artists’ books. 121 Nurses compiles the pulp nurse-romance paperbacks whose lurid covers Richard Prince scanned and reworked for his celebrated Nurse Paintings (2002–2008). The book is itself an appropriation: it borrows its design from Prince’s own 136 Nurses, the catalogue raisonné of those paintings — so Doeringer appropriates the source material Prince appropriated, and the form in which Prince catalogued it, folding authorship back on itself. Offset-printed in Los Angeles, 42 pages, perfect-bound, 21.5 × 14 cm. Issued without ISBN in the tradition of the artist’s book and zine.

title: Records
description: Eric Doeringer’s remake of Ed Ruscha’s 1971 classic Records, and a companion in method to his other appropriations. Ruscha’s original reproduced thirty records from his own collection, each spread pairing an album cover on the left with a photograph of the bare vinyl LP on the right. To make his version, Doeringer (b. 1974) tracked down copies of every record Ruscha had pictured and re-photographed them in the same sequence — but the two books are pointedly not identical: his copies carry their own histories of wear, price stickers, and doodles, and the labels differ in mono/stereo pressings and reissues. The result turns a reproduction into a meditation on collecting, difference, and the impossibility of a true copy. It belongs to the now-sizeable genre of Ruscha-homage artists’ books — Doeringer has also remade Some Los Angeles Apartments, Real Estate Opportunities, and Stained. Self-published under his Copycat Publications imprint in an edition of 1,000, signed on the title page; softcover, 72 pages, 7 × 5.5 in.

title: David King Publications 1977–2019
publisher: Colpa Press / San Francisco Center for the Book
description: The first published survey of the book projects and graphic design of David King (1948–2019), the English-born, New York– and San Francisco–based artist, designer, and musician best known for creating the Crass symbol. King moved to New York in 1977 and made hundreds of flyers for clubs such as Danceteria, Pravda, and the Peppermint Lounge while playing in the no wave band Arsenal; relocating to San Francisco in 1980, he designed for the I-Beam and played in the post-punk groups Sleeping Dogs and Brain Rust. Across four decades he produced dozens of cheaply made Xerox and offset zines — Suburbs of Hell, Too Many Zombies, Sleeping Dogs — collaging appropriated images from mainstream magazines, and, later, idiosyncratic small-run books issued through Colpa Press, &Pens, and Gingko Press. This 120-page volume, co-published by Colpa Press and the San Francisco Center for the Book, gathers that work with an introduction by Matt Borruso and an essay by the design studio Experimental Jetset. It accompanied the first survey exhibitions of King’s output, at the San Francisco Center for the Book (October 25–December 22, 2024) and Printed Matter, New York (June 5–August 24, 2025). Not to be confused with the British graphic designer David King (1943–2016) of Soviet-design fame.

title: Record Culture Magazine Issue 11
description:
Record is a biannual print journal on the people at the center of the world’s niche music communities and the places those scenes meet art, fashion, and design; Issue 11 (2026) runs 208 pages plus two bound supplements.

Built on candid longform interviews and photography made in its subjects’ homes and studios, the issue gathers conversations with Paul Takahashi, Nicolas Godin, Kiki Kudo, Jean Touitou, Ariel Zetina, OKO DJ, Sound Metaphors, and Fraser Cooke, among others, alongside Luke Jenner’s short story Plant Bar and the visual feature Eddie Ruscha: Sound / Waves. Two saddle-stitched booklets accompany the perfect-bound main magazine: The Invitations of Life... Child!, drawn from Nicky Siano’s Gallery-era archive (52 pages), and You Can Hear Your Own Heartbeat: A Day at Audio-Technica, photographed by Kento Mori (60 pages).

Founded in 2016 in New York’s Chinatown and now made across New York, Berlin, and Melbourne with its publisher in Cork, Ireland, Record pairs archival features on musical ephemera with original illustration and design under art director Holly Canham. Issue 11 continues the magazine’s approach of treating record culture as a lens on wider visual and social life rather than as genre coverage.

title: Index
binding: 11 saddle-stitched softcover books in a silkscreened fluted slipcase
description:
The first-edition boxed set of Index, the career-spanning self-anthology by the Magnum photographer Christopher Anderson (b. 1970) — eleven saddle-stitched volumes housed in a silkscreened fluted slipcase, published by STANLEY/BARKER in 2026 and designed by Brian Roettinger.

Rather than a linear retrospective, Index breaks three decades of work into eleven separate booklets — Afghanistan, Haiti, China, France, Cars, Self Portrait, Holiday, New York, Trouble, White House, and 9 East 71st Street — that can be read in any order, juxtaposing war, migration, politics, and domestic intimacy like entries in an index. The 320-page set measures 255 × 225 mm; this copy is signed by Anderson.

Anderson won the Robert Capa Gold Medal in 1999 for photographs made aboard a sinking boat of Haitian migrants bound for the United States, then covered Afghanistan, Iraq, and Israel/Palestine before turning toward family, cities, and self-portraiture — work that moves fluidly between reportage and the personal. A member of Magnum Photos, he built the monographs Capitolio, Son, Stump, and Approximate Joy; Index draws that full arc together and was widely noted on release, including in The Guardian and Le Monde.

title: Folk Songs
description:
The catalogue for Folk Songs, Richard Prince's 2025 exhibition at Gagosian in New York — a 136-page softcover with a die-cut reproduction of one of the paintings tipped into its kraft cover.

Published by Gagosian in 2026 to accompany the show at 555 West 24th Street (November 6–December 20, 2025), the book documents handmade paintings, drawings, and collages made between 2018 and 2023 together with five sculptures dating from 2007 to 2025, reproduced in color plates and installation views. An essay by the art historian Sydney Stutterheim reads Prince's recurring methods — self-reference and appropriation, buried meanings and apocrypha — against a palette of soft pinks, magentas, and reds set against black. Designed by Graphic Thought Facility, London, and printed by Pureprint.

Richard Prince (b. 1949) is among the central figures of the Pictures Generation, whose rephotographed Marlboro Cowboys, Nurse paintings, joke canvases, and Instagram New Portraits made appropriation a defining strategy of postwar art. His work is held by the Museum of Modern Art, the Whitney, the Guggenheim, and Tate; Folk Songs extends the looser, hand-made register of his recent painting.

title: Gary Schneider: Portraits
contributors: Deborah Martin Kao (Author of text and interview with the artist)
description:
The first major study of Gary Schneider (b. 1954), the South African-born New York photographer whose long-exposure, flashlight-drawn portraits reimagine photographic likeness as a record of time and collaboration.

Written by Deborah Martin Kao, the Richard L. Menschel Curator of Photography at Harvard's Fogg Art Museum, the catalogue traces two decades of Schneider's portrait work: his re-presentations of nineteenth-century studio negatives, his life-size handprint photograms, and his fragmented face portraits, made by moving a light pen across a sitter's features during exposures that can last more than an hour. Kao also examines the scientific collaborations behind his images of blood, DNA, and hair, and closes with an extended interview with the artist. Yale University Press published it in association with the Harvard University Art Museums to accompany the retrospective at the Arthur M. Sackler Museum (28 February to 23 May 2004). Paperback, 122 pages, with 103 color and 49 black-and-white plates.

Schneider trained at the Michaelis School of Fine Art in Cape Town and at Pratt Institute, and has lived in New York since 1977, where in 1981 he co-founded the master printing lab Schneider/Erdman. His Genetic Self-Portrait (1998) and ongoing Nudes series pushed portraiture toward science and abstraction, and his work is held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Whitney Museum of American Art, and the Art Institute of Chicago. He printed for many photographers, among them Peter Hujar, whose negatives are the subject of his 2024 memoir Peter Hujar: Behind the Camera and In the Darkroom.

title: Index
editor: Willem de Rooij, Axel Wieder, Susanne Gaensheimer
description:
An inquiry into the iconography of protest by the Dutch conceptual artist Willem de Rooij (b. 1969), Index compiles some 500 newspaper images of protest marches and collective mourning collected between 1999 and 2002.

The photographs, cut from daily newspapers over three years, were first organized in 2002 into eighteen framed panels arranged chronologically as Index: Riots, Protest, Mourning and Commemoration (as represented in newspapers, January 2000–July 2002). This 508-page artist's book reorganizes the complete series for the printed page, returning the images to the mass-circulation form in which they first appeared and documenting a way of working — clipping from print — that the shift to online image culture has made obsolete. It was published with essays by Sven Lütticken and Pablo Martínez on the occasion of exhibitions at Arnolfini, Bristol (2014–15) and MMK Museum für Moderne Kunst, Frankfurt (2016–17), co-published by the two institutions with Verlag der Buchhandlung Walther König, Cologne.

De Rooij studied at the Gerrit Rietveld Academie and the Rijksakademie in Amsterdam and worked collaboratively with Jeroen de Rijke as De Rijke/De Rooij from 1994 to 2006, representing the Netherlands at the 2005 Venice Biennale. Professor of fine art at Frankfurt's Städelschule since 2006, he works across film, installation, and textile, and is represented by Petzel Gallery, New York, and Regen Projects, Los Angeles.

title: Ray Johnson
description:
A monograph on the collagist and mail-art pioneer Ray Johnson (1927–1995), presenting 42 collages made between 1966 and 1994 — most never previously exhibited or published — with a new essay by the writer and biographer Brad Gooch.

Published by Matthew Marks Gallery in 2017, the clothbound volume reproduces Johnson's most expansive work in 87 plates: layered compositions of magazine clippings, photographs, and hand-worked elements that merge art history with celebrity, word with image, and the personal with the universal. Gooch's essay traces a practice delivering, in his words, "surprise and joy, excitement and entertainment," likening the collages to jokes sublimely told by a tortured stand-up comedian.

A Black Mountain College alumnus who turned from painting to collage after moving to New York in 1949, Johnson became a seminal Pop artist, a proto-conceptualist, and the founder of the New York Correspondance School, distributing his work through the postal service — by 1965 he was known as "New York's most famous unknown artist." The library also holds Ray Johnson c/o, the Art Institute of Chicago's 2021 survey of his correspondence art.

title: 1954 Drawings on a Bus, Sketchbook 23
description:
A facsimile of Sketchbook 23 by the American painter Ellsworth Kelly (1923–2015), reproducing the ink drawings of shifting shadow patterns he made riding New York City buses in the fall of 1954, weeks after returning from six years in Paris.

In Paris, Kelly had built paintings from window patterns and the shadows cast by Seine bridges; back in New York he sketched the sunlight moving across bus seat backs and overhead bars, then reworked the sketches in the studio into abstractions stripped of their physical source. These drawings fed directly into his earliest American paintings, among them Atlantic (1956), the first of his works to enter a museum collection when the Whitney purchased it in 1957. The sketchbook itself has an unusual origin: a friend gave Kelly a blank publisher's dummy of Sigfried Giedion's 1928 Bauen in Frankreich, its cover designed by Moholy-Nagy, and the facsimile reproduces that cover. Co-published by Matthew Marks Gallery and Steidl in 2007 as a slipcased hardcover with a 2006 text by the artist, accompanying the gallery's exhibition of twenty drawings from the sketchbook.

Kelly stands among the defining figures of postwar American abstraction, his hard-edge shape and color paintings drawn from observed fragments of the world. His work is held by MoMA, the Whitney, and Tate, among others, and his estate is represented by Matthew Marks Gallery.

title: Visible World
description:
An encyclopedic artist's book by the Zurich duo Peter Fischli (b. 1952) and David Weiss (1946–2012), Visible World compresses 2,848 color photographs taken over fifteen years of travel into 260 flexibound pages — the world rendered as a deadpan, seemingly total inventory.

Conceived and designed by the artists and co-published by Matthew Marks Gallery and Buchhandlung Walther König in 2000, the book is the printed form of their long-running Sichtbare Welt project, which the duo also presented as photographs on light tables. Airports, beaches, gardens, mountains, and cities pass in tight grids without hierarchy or commentary, extending the taxonomic impulse of their 1982 publication Suddenly this Overview. The pictures court the generic — sunsets and tourist views done straight — so that the book reads at once as archive, travelogue, and gentle parody of both.

Working together from 1979 until Weiss's death in 2012, Fischli and Weiss built one of contemporary art's most influential collaborative bodies of work, spanning the film The Way Things Go (1987), the clay Suddenly this Overview sculptures, and the retrospective How to Work Better at the Guggenheim (2016). The library holds several of their other titles, including 800 Views of Airports and How to Work Better.
tags: Art, Photography, Conceptual Art, Artist Books, Travel Photography

title: On Any Given Day in Spring / Light Balances
description:
A quiet two-volume set of late photographs by Robert Adams (b. 1937), the central chronicler of the American West's transformation, published as paired paperbacks in a plain cardboard slipcase by Matthew Marks Gallery and Fraenkel Gallery in 2012.

On Any Given Day in Spring (32 pages, 30 plates) follows seabirds, sand, ocean, and sky at North Beach on Washington's coast — encounters Adams describes as "less an answer to our questions than a rephrasing of them," adding that "there is no certainty, on any given day in spring, that the birds will be there." Light Balances (48 pages, 57 plates) records light filtering through the foliage of a protected forest near the Columbia River estuary in Astoria, Oregon, where Adams has lived since 1997. Both books hold to his spare black-and-white attentiveness, here turned from the developed landscapes of his New Topographics years toward what remains intact.

Adams came to prominence in the 1975 New Topographics exhibition and received the Hasselblad Award in 2009; his retrospective The Place We Live toured internationally from Yale University Art Gallery. He is represented by Fraenkel Gallery and Matthew Marks Gallery. The library also holds his Gone? (Steidl, 2010).

title: Mr. Remember
editor: Lærke Rydal Jørgensen, Mathias Ussing Seeberg, William Pym, Alex Da Corte
contributors: Poul Erik Tøjner (Foreword); Bruce Hainley (Essay); Delia Solomons (Essay); Sarah Nicole Prickett (Essay); Steven Zultanski (Essay); Derek McCormack (Essay)
description:
The comprehensive monograph on the Philadelphia-based installation artist Alex Da Corte (b. 1980), published for Mr. Remember, his major European retrospective at the Louisiana Museum of Modern Art (July 14, 2022 – January 8, 2023).

Documenting all of Da Corte's major works to date, the book matches his high-production, ultra-chromatic sensibility: a three-color cloth binding with silver foil on the cover, 200 color and 50 duotone plates, more than 100 pages of installation views, and a paperback volume sewn into the binding. The Louisiana retrospective staged his Day-Glo paintings, sculptures, videos, and scenographies — colored walls, neon, even scent — around works like Rubber Pencil Devil, the 57-part film in which the artist impersonates figures from American children's television. Edited by Lærke Rydal Jørgensen, Mathias Ussing Seeberg, William Pym, and the artist, with a foreword by Poul Erik Tøjner and texts by Bruce Hainley, Delia Solomons, Sarah Nicole Prickett, Steven Zultanski, Derek McCormack, and others.

Rooted in American popular culture — as a teenager he planned to animate for Disney — Da Corte builds seductive, uncanny worlds from consumer imagery, appearing in his own films as Popeye, the Statue of Liberty, Mister Rogers, or Eminem. His 2021 Met Roof Garden commission As Long as the Sun Lasts brought the work wide attention. The library holds six of his other titles, including Rubber Pencil Devil and Free Roses.

notes: Three-color cloth binding with silver foil; paperback supplement sewn in. Danish publication December 2022; US trade release March 2023 via DAP. Seventh Alex Da Corte title in the collection. Summer acquisitions and archiving 2026. Accessioned 2026-07-23.

title: Ellsworth Kelly in San Francisco
publisher: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art / University of California Press
contributors: Madeleine Grynsztejn (Essay); Julian Myers (Essay); Neal Benezra (Foreword)
description:
The catalog for Ellsworth Kelly in San Francisco, SFMOMA's 2002–03 exhibition uniting the twenty-two works the museum acquired from the artist's personal collection in 1999 — including Cité (1951), Red Blue (1966), and Curve XXI (1978–80) — with its earlier holdings, together the most important grouping of Ellsworth Kelly's work in any museum.

Spanning fifty years of paintings, sculptures, collages, drawings, and reliefs drawn from the museum and Bay Area private collections, the exhibition (July 13, 2002 – January 5, 2003) presented 58 works in all. The primary essay by Madeleine Grynsztejn, SFMOMA's Elise S. Haas Senior Curator of Painting and Sculpture and the show's organizer, follows the evolution of Kelly's art, his interest in the phenomenology of vision, and his chance-generated compositions; Julian Myers contributes analyses of key works and groupings, from the early figural paintings to the shaped panels and reliefs, with a foreword by Neal Benezra. Co-published with University of California Press.

Kelly (1923–2015) was a defining figure of postwar American abstraction, his hard-edge shape and color paintings drawn from observed fragments of the world. The library also holds 1954 Drawings on a Bus, Sketchbook 23, the facsimile of the sketchbook behind his earliest American paintings.

title: Sarah Morris
publisher: EMMA – Espoo Museum of Modern Art
editor: Pilvi Kalhama, Ari Karttunen, Milla Rissanen, Pernilla Wiik
description:
The catalog for the British-American artist Sarah Morris's (b. 1967) solo exhibition at EMMA – Espoo Museum of Modern Art (June 21, 2017 – January 7, 2018), documenting the abstract paintings and films of an artist who treats the two media as one continuous practice.

The exhibition brought together three of Morris's films, a selection of her graphic, hard-color paintings, and Mäntyjä (Pines), a 30-meter site-specific wall painting created for EMMA's Aalto-influenced Tapiola setting. Since the mid-1990s Morris has traced the tension between social space, identity, and power, reading cities — Paris, Rio de Janeiro, Beijing — through their architectures, logos, and systems of control. The 175-page hardcover, edited by museum director Pilvi Kalhama with Ari Karttunen, Milla Rissanen, and Pernilla Wiik, includes color illustrations throughout and, unusually, music notation. Published by EMMA in 2019.

Morris lives and works in New York; her paintings and films are held by MoMA, Tate, and the Centre Pompidou, and she is represented by White Cube, Capitain Petzel, and Air de Paris.

title: Neue Malerei
contributors: Markus Bertsch (Essay); Simon Elson (Essay); Florian Illies (Essay)
description:
A conceptual inversion of the painting catalog by the German artist Christian Jankowski (b. 1968), Neue Malerei — "new painting" — presents oil canvases of works by Picasso, Richter, Warhol, Dürer, and other icons of art history, painted by an artist who, by his own admission, cannot paint at all.

Jankowski collected photographs of tableaux vivants found on the internet — people restaging famous paintings — and sent them to his studio in Shenzhen, where Chinese copy painters rendered them in oil on canvas. The catalog, published for his March 2018 exhibition at the Berlin auction house Grisebach, plays the result straight, in linen-bound quarto with texts by Markus Bertsch, Simon Elson, and Florian Illies. As Illies writes, "Nothing is right on the (following) pages of this catalog. Everything is shaking — the optics, the habits of seeing, the certainties, the standards of quality." It is a book of new painting in which we only see works of old masters. In German; distributed by Walther König.

Jankowski works in video, performance, and installation built on collaborations with non-art professionals — TV fortune tellers, magicians, weightlifters — probing how art passes through mass media. He curated Manifesta 11 in Zurich (2016), teaches at the Stuttgart Academy, and is represented by Petzel Gallery, New York.

notes: Text in German. Distributed by Verlag der Buchhandlung Walther König. First Christian Jankowski title in the collection. Summer acquisitions and archiving 2026. Accessioned 2026-07-23.

title: Nude and Landscape
contributors: Elizabeth Manchester (Essay); Sid Sachs (Essay); William Horner (Interview)
description:
A catalog that reads the British collagist John Stezaker (b. 1949) against art-historical tradition — landscape painting and the nude — rather than the cinematic imagery his found-image work is best known for.

Centered on works from the 1980s onward, when Stezaker turned from the culture of the image to the nature of the image, the book presents his Bridge collages and the anatomical nudes of the Fall and Expulsion series, including many works never previously shown. Most telling is its inclusion of unaltered found images — postcards and plates so close to the finished collages that only the absence or presence of the artist's cut distinguishes them, laying the methodology bare. Published by Ridinghouse with the Rosenwald-Wolf Gallery for the exhibition curated by Sid Sachs at the University of the Arts, Philadelphia (October 13 – November 19, 2011), later restaged at Petzel Gallery, New York (2013). With texts by Elizabeth Manchester and Sachs, and a conversation between Stezaker and William Horner.

Stezaker came to prominence among the British conceptualists of the 1970s and received the Deutsche Börse Photography Prize in 2012, following his 2011 Whitechapel Gallery retrospective. He is represented by The Approach, London, and Petzel Gallery, New York. The library also holds the Rubell Family Collection volume on his work.

notes: Published by Ridinghouse in association with Rosenwald-Wolf Gallery; DAP lists March 2012 publication, some sources say 2013. Second John Stezaker title in the collection. Summer acquisitions and archiving 2026. Accessioned 2026-07-23.

title: Crease Folds
description:
A pocket-sized artist's book by the British-American painter and filmmaker Sarah Morris (b. 1967), Crease Folds chronicles — in reality and in fiction — the period in which she made the film Strange Magic (2014).

Strange Magic surveys the Louis Vuitton empire's production of luxury goods — fashion, fragrance, champagne, architecture — as the capital source behind the Frank Gehry-designed Fondation Louis Vuitton, deconstructing the mechanisms of that cultural currency and the fantasy inherent in luxury itself. For the book, Morris juxtaposed this making-of material with an invented counterpart: after meeting the Oscar-winning Pulp Fiction screenwriter Roger Avary at the 2012 Locarno Film Festival, where an homage to her films was presented, she asked him to write a fictional text about her. The 120-page softcover, edited by the artist and published by Ivorypress LiberArs, Madrid, in 2015, sets fiction and fantasy against the record of an artwork's production.

Morris's paintings and city films — Paris, Rio, Beijing — trace the codes of social space and power. Her work is held by MoMA, Tate, and the Centre Pompidou; she is represented by White Cube, Capitain Petzel, and Air de Paris. The library also holds the EMMA – Espoo Museum of Modern Art catalog of her 2017–18 retrospective.

title: Silkscreens
description:
The first comprehensive gathering of the silkscreens of John Stezaker (b. 1949) — a side of the British collagist little known next to his small, intimate collages of film stills and postcards.

Spanning 1977 to 1994, the mid- to large-scale silkscreens work Stezaker's found imagery at the scale of painting: manipulated kissing couples, disembodied men and women, floating baby-heads, and film stills, estranged through enlargement and repetition. Caoimhín Mac Giolla Léith's essay is the first text to consider the silkscreens as a whole body of work. The 144-page volume, with 85 color illustrations, was published by Ridinghouse with Galerie Gisela Capitain, Cologne; Friedrich Petzel Gallery, New York; and The Approach, London, on the occasion of John Stezaker: Silkscreens at Capitain Petzel, Berlin (September 18 – October 30, 2010).

Stezaker came to prominence among the British conceptualists of the 1970s and received the Deutsche Börse Photography Prize in 2012, following his 2011 Whitechapel Gallery retrospective. He is represented by The Approach and Petzel Gallery. This is the third Stezaker title in the library, alongside Nude and Landscape and the Rubell Family Collection volume.

title: One on One
publisher: Ridinghouse / Tel Aviv Museum of Art
contributors: Irith Hadar (Essay); Dalit Matatyahu (Essay); Suzanne Landau (Foreword); Christophe Gallois (Interview); Daniel F. Herrmann (Interview)
description:

title: Révélations: Iconographie de la Salpêtrière, Paris 1875–1918

description: Révélations presents one of the earliest and most significant photographic archives in the history of clinical psychiatry. Compiled and edited by contemporary photographer and designer Javier Viver, this publication draws from over 4,000 photographs and thirty-two volumes that were systematically produced between 1875 and 1918 at the Salpêtrière Hospital in Paris. Under the direction of Jean-Martin Charcot—founder of modern neurology—and financed by the French government, the hospital's archive represented an unprecedented effort to document and categorize patients through innovative photographic-documentary techniques. The archive reveals the complex intersection of medical science and public spectacle. Tuesday sessions at the Salpêtrière became celebrated events for Paris's cultural elite, where Charcot conducted demonstrations involving hypnosis-induced displays of patients. The photographic record reveals how emerging medical understanding became entangled with theatrical presentation.

description: "Script of Demolition" documents the visual methodology behind controlled industrial demolitions through an examination of the Fink family demolition company's 60-year archive. By appropriating and recontextualizing these utilitarian industrial archives, Schmuch examines the relationship between visual documentation, planning, and reality.

title: 101 Tragedies of Enrique Metinides
description: "101 Tragedies" represents Enrique Metinides's personal selection of 101 key images from over 50 years spent documenting crime scenes, accidents, and catastrophes throughout Mexico City. This integration of archival material creates a hybrid document that contextualizes Metinides's work within its original journalistic form. Ziff contributes an interpretive essay exploring Metinides's life, artistic vision, and significance within Mexican photojournalism.

title: The Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death
binding: Hardcover with black cloth boards and black pictorial dust jacket
description: "The Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death" documents the remarkable career and legacy of Frances Glessner Lee, a pioneering forensic scientist and philanthropist who revolutionized crime scene investigation training. Published in 2004 with 225 pages of lush color photography and specially prepared line drawings, Corinne May Botz's book presents an extraordinary visual and narrative exploration of Lee's eighteen miniature crime-scene dioramas created in the 1940s and 1950s. Built at a precise scale of 1:12 (one inch to one foot), these hyperrealistic dollhouse-sized models display meticulous attention to forensic detail: working doors and windows, carefully placed clues such as overturned ashtrays and bullet holes in walls, ligature marks painted on doll figures, and decomposition effects rendered with scientific accuracy. Each diorama cost between $3,000-$4,500 to construct and represents a composite based on actual case files. Botz's accompanying essay, drawing from archival research and interviews with Lee's family and police colleagues, provides biographical context.

notes: Frances Glessner Lee (1878-1962) was the first female police captain in the United States and is known as the "mother of forensic science." In 1931, she helped establish Harvard's Department of Legal Medicine—the only such forensic program existing in North America at that time—and in 1936 she endowed the department with a substantial gift of $250,000. Lee's Nutshell Studies are now housed at the Maryland Office of the Chief Medical Examiner in Baltimore, where they continue to serve as active educational tools in annual forensic investigation seminars. The dioramas were designed to teach homicide investigators to "convict the guilty, clear the innocent, and find the truth in a nutshell." description: Sarah Pickering's "Explosions, Fires, and Public Order" documents four interconnected photographic series exploring the secretive spaces where civil defense and emergency preparedness training takes place. Pickering's "Fire Series" and "Incident" were produced during her artist-in-residence at the UK Fire Training College, where she photographed both active training fires set inside meticulously constructed home interiors and the stark, charred remnants after blazes were extinguished.

description: Arnold Odermatt spent over four decades as a Swiss police photographer in the canton of Nidwalden, documenting automobile accidents from 1948 to 1990. Unlike typical documentary police photography, Odermatt's images reveal a sophisticated artistic sensibility, combining clinical attention to detail with an aesthetic appreciation for composition and landscape. His photographs transform scenes of destruction into unexpectedly haunting and sometimes surreal visual narratives, capturing damaged vehicles as sculptural objects arranged in the Alpine landscape. The work captures consequences of excessive speed, impaired driving, and traffic violations across four decades, presenting melancholic, sometimes darkly comedic, and always atmospheric moments that explore themes of human fragility and societal risk.

title: Selected Collages
description:
Published on the occasion of Thomas Eggerer's 2022 survey at 15 Orient, Selected Collages, 2002 to 2022 gathers two decades of the collage practice that runs beneath the painter's better-known canvases, where his figures in public space first take shape.

The softcover volume, produced with Brooklyn's Inpatient Press, reproduces collages built from Eggerer's archive of found printed matter: high-gloss 1980s university yearbooks, illustrated fitness manuals, self-help guides, nature books, and a favored 1982 Italian volume on the Milan subway. Cut-out photographs, he writes, rest in a box "until I feel more interested in them, which can sometimes take years"; the source has to be "almost normal, not too sensational." An essay by art historian David Joselit accompanies the plates across 90 pages. The exhibition ran at 15 Orient, Brooklyn, from September 7 to October 8, 2022.

Eggerer (b. 1963, Munich) trained as a painter at the Art Academy in Munich and moved to New York in 1994, where he joined the collective Group Material. Represented by Petzel Gallery and Galerie Buchholz, he has exhibited at the Frans Hals Museum, Kunstverein Braunschweig, and the Wadsworth Atheneum, and his work is held by the Museum of Modern Art, the Whitney Museum, SFMOMA, and the Stedelijk Museum, Amsterdam.

title: Chapter 5
description:
Chapter 5 is the fifth installment in the long-running collaborative book series by Rita Ackermann and Andro Wekua, published by Nieves, Zurich, in 2026, its photocopy-style cover collaging the numerals 2, 3, and 5 so the title reads as Chapter 235.

The Chapter books began after the two artists met in 2002, unfolding as a correspondence in print: part visual diary, part exchange of drawings, collages, and fragments of text that drift between figuration and abstraction. The series moved from a self-published Chapter 1 to Nieves editions of Chapter 2 and Chapter 3 (both 2004), then to Chapter 4 (Fergus McCaffrey and Case Publishing, 2021). This volume returns the series to Nieves as 64 pages of black-and-white offset imagery without text, accumulating impressions of memory and distance rather than resolving into fixed narrative.

Rita Ackermann (b. 1968, Budapest) is a Hungarian-American painter, represented by Hauser & Wirth, whose process-driven canvases layer painting, drawing, and collage. Andro Wekua (b. 1977, Sokhumi, Georgia), represented by Gladstone and Sprüth Magers, works across painting, sculpture, film, and installation, with exhibitions at Kunsthalle Basel, Museo Tamayo, and the Venice Biennale.

title: David Weiss: Works, 1968–1979
contributors: Hans Ulrich Obrist (Text); Urs Lüthi (Text); Douglas Fogle (Essay)
description:
Before Fischli/Weiss there was a decade of David Weiss working alone, filling notebooks and sheets of paper with drawings that stayed hidden for more than thirty years.

Published by the Swiss Institute with Karma in 2016, this compact hardcover gathers the works on paper Weiss made between 1968 and 1979: cartoon imagery, ethereal abstractions and electric cityscapes, together with previously unpublished writings. Edited by Karen Marta and Simon Castets, the book pairs intimate recollections from Weiss's friends Urs Lüthi and Hans Ulrich Obrist with an essay by curator Douglas Fogle tracing the influences on the early work, from Robert Walser to Bugs Bunny. It follows the exhibitions at the Bündner Kunstmuseum in Chur (2014) and Swiss Institute, New York (2014–15), made possible only because Weiss, in the months before his death, began organizing the notebooks and early drawings he had set aside when the collaboration began.

Weiss (1946–2012) joined Peter Fischli in 1979 to form Fischli/Weiss, the duo behind Der Lauf der Dinge and one of contemporary art's most inventive bodies of work, honored with a Guggenheim retrospective in 2016. This volume restores the solo artist behind the partnership, and it sits alongside the many Fischli & Weiss titles held in this library.

title: Jack Pierson
binding: Pocket-size edition; cover carries only the artist's name and title, no other markings; binding unverified
description:
A pocket-sized book on Jack Pierson published by Photology, the Milan photography gallery that has represented his photographs since 1999, on the occasion of his solo exhibition there in the spring of 2001. Barely bigger than a postcard, it carries nothing on its cover but the artist's name and the title, and nothing else anywhere: no ISBN, no barcode, no apparatus. The gallery would later describe it simply as its best-selling pocket size edition.

The artist's official bibliography credits the volume with a text by the poet Eileen Myles, Pierson's longtime friend and interpreter. The intimate scale suits his registers: longing, faded glamour, male beauty and out-of-focus American light. Photology returned to the artist around 2008 with a larger ISBN'd hardcover surveying some sixty works across media; this small, scarce volume is its predecessor.

Pierson (b. 1960, Plymouth, Massachusetts) emerged from the Boston School alongside Nan Goldin, David Armstrong and Mark Morrisroe, and is best known for photographs steeped in longing and faded Americana and for the word sculptures, begun in 1991, that he assembles from salvaged signage letters. His Self-Portrait series appeared in the 2004 Whitney Biennial; long represented by Cheim & Read, he now shows with Lisson Gallery.

title: Fotografías
description:
A darkened carnival cosmos, photographed at the edge of legibility.

Fotografías gathers 92 black-and-white photographs of the garish fantasy scenes Peter Fischli and David Weiss found painted on fairground attractions: shooting galleries, ghost trains, carousel panels and motorcycle fuel tanks, collected over years of travel through Switzerland and abroad. Shot on black-and-white slide film deliberately underexposed by two to three stops and printed at snapshot size, the pictures subdue their kitsch sources into murky, haunting nocturnes. Romantic sunsets, mystical mountains, wild boars, clowns and doe-eyed girls become small, dark, emotionally charged icons. The book, published by Walther König to accompany the 2005 exhibition at Galerie Eva Presenhuber, Zurich, carries no text beyond its title page, letting the sequence of images do all the work.

Fischli and Weiss collaborated from 1979 until Weiss's death in 2012, building a body of work, from the film The Way Things Go to the encyclopedic Visible World, that dignifies the overlooked and levels the distinction between high and low art, a project surveyed in the Guggenheim's 2016 retrospective How to Work Better. Fotografías is among their most distilled statements: vernacular painting remade as fine art through nothing more than exposure and scale.

title: The New York Times Paintings: November – December 2015
description:
A catalog for the exhibition that turned the daily front page of record into painting.

Published by Petzel to accompany The New York Times Paintings: November – December 2015 (November 10, 2016 – January 14, 2017), the book documents a body of work made from screenshots of the nytimes.com homepage captured over two months in late 2015. Guyton fed the files through an Epson 9900 large-format printer in UltraChrome HDR ink on linen, producing 84-by-69-inch canvases where headlines about terror, climate, and the coming election sit beside sidebar ads and navigation bars, complete with the glitches, streaks, and misregistrations the printer introduces. Edited by Jessica Li and designed by Joseph Logan, the 80-page volume pairs plates of the paintings with installation views of Petzel's uptown townhouse galleries; the show opened, pointedly, two days after the 2016 presidential election.

Wade Guyton (b. 1972, Hammond, Indiana) has made paintings since the early 2000s by dragging folded linen through inkjet printers, letting the machine's errors stand as the work's mark-making. The Whitney Museum surveyed the work in Wade Guyton OS in 2012; long affiliated with Petzel and Galerie Gisela Capitain, he now shows with Matthew Marks Gallery and Galerie Chantal Crousel.

title: Life with P.
description:
Life with P.: Journals, 1966–1976 presents the previously unpublished journals of poet and painter Musa McKim Guston, an intimate decade-long record of daily life with her husband Philip Guston — "P." in her private shorthand — kept during the most consequential turn of his career.

Spanning 1966 to 1976, the entries move between the couple's home in Woodstock, visits to New York, artist residencies and travels to Mexico and Italy, tracing the years in which Guston abandoned abstraction for the cartoon-inflected figuration of his late work. Edited by Sara Harrison and Musa Mayer, the 432-page hardback interleaves McKim's journals and poems with 230 color illustrations of artworks and archival photographs, framed by an introduction and contextual notes by Mayer.

McKim (1908–1992) was an artist in her own right: a painting student at the Otis Art Institute when she met Guston, a collaborator on his WPA-era murals, and later a poet whose verses he embellished in their joint "Poem Pictures." Mayer, the couple's daughter and president of The Guston Foundation, extends the account begun in her 1988 memoir Night Studio. The book appeared alongside the Hauser & Wirth New York exhibition "Life With P. – Philip Guston: Paintings and Drawings 1964–1978."

title: Time Travel
description:
Time travel, in this catalog, is less a conceit than a method: hang a Canaletto near a Cindy Sherman and watch four centuries collapse into a single conversation.

Published on the occasion of the two-part exhibition at Petzel's Upper East Side townhouse (November 15, 2023 through February 10, 2024), the catalog records an unusual collaboration between the New York contemporary gallery and DYS 44 Lampronti Gallery, the London dealership in Italian Old Masters. The parlor floor held works from the sixteenth through nineteenth centuries, among them Artemisia Gentileschi's Bathsheba at her bath, Canaletto's The Prisons of St Mark, Domenico Remps's trompe-l'oeil Cabinet of Curiosities, and canvases by Guercino, Ribera, and Cagnacci, while the third floor gathered contemporary responses from John Currin, Cindy Sherman, Jeff Koons, Jutta Koether, Roe Ethridge, Emily Mae Smith, and Emma Webster.

The pairings argue that the Baroque's cinematic drama, its oscillation between sacred and profane, remains a living vocabulary. Koons's Gazing Ball and Sherman's history-portrait photography read here not as quotation but as continuation, mapping the masters' stylized theatricality onto the present moment.

title: How to See Like a Machine: Images After AI
description:
In How to See Like a Machine: Images After AI, the artist and geographer Trevor Paglen argues that photography’s basic terms have flipped: images are now made by machines, for machines, and the picture that once waited to be seen has started looking back.

Collecting essays written over roughly fifteen years, the book tracks the shift from human to machine vision: the training-image economy laid bare in Paglen’s Excavating AI research, and generative models now producing pictures indistinguishable from photographs. Chapters range from psyops and UFO photography to stage magic and public relations, arguing these seemingly alien systems are stranger, and more human, than they appear. Published by Verso in May 2026 as a 192-page hardback, it is Paglen’s sixth book.

Paglen (b. 1974, Camp Springs, Maryland) trained as a geographer at UC Berkeley and has spent two decades making the hidden infrastructures of surveillance and machine perception visible through photography, sculpture, and investigative research. A 2017 MacArthur Fellow, he showed for years with San Francisco’s Altman Siegel (closed 2025) and is now represented by Pace Gallery; his work is held by SFMOMA, the Metropolitan Museum, and the Smithsonian American Art Museum, which surveyed his career in the 2018 retrospective Sites Unseen.

title: Adversarially Evolved Hallucinations
description:
Trevor Paglen’s Adversarially Evolved Hallucinations (2017–ongoing) treats machine hallucination not as a glitch but as the defining condition of AI-made images—and this slim critical reader, volume four in Sternberg Press’s Research/Practice series, unpacks what that means.

Edited by Anthony Downey, the book pairs a conversation between Paglen and Downey with Downey’s essay “The Return of the Uncanny: Artificial Intelligence and Estranged Futures.” Paglen describes training neural networks on invented corpora, then prompting a second network to hallucinate images from what it has learned to “see,” yielding uncanny prints like Vampire (Corpus: Monsters of Capitalism). Downey argues AI’s lack of embodied experience means it can only produce estranged, allegorical pictures of the world.

Paglen (b. 1974, Camp Springs, Maryland) is an American artist and geographer whose work exposes the infrastructures of state secrecy, surveillance, and machine vision. A 2017 MacArthur Fellow, he has shown at the Smithsonian American Art Museum and the Barbican, with work held by MoMA and the Whitney. The volume extends an inquiry into AI classification running from ImageNet Roulette (2019, with Kate Crawford) to his 2026 book How to See Like a Machine: Images After AI.

title: I Could Tell You But Then You Would Have to Be Destroyed By Me: Emblems from the Pentagon's Black World

description:
Trevor Paglen's I Could Tell You But Then You Would Have to Be Destroyed by Me collects more than seventy insignia patches worn on classified U.S. military and intelligence programs, reading their cartoonish, occult imagery as an accidental portrait of the government's secret world.

Assembled through Freedom of Information Act requests and tips from current and former operators, the book reproduces each patch in full color with Paglen's decoding of its symbolism: a grey alien captioned "to serve man," six-pointed stars standing in for Area 51, red stars marking Nevada test ranges, and mottoes too obscene to print. This 2010 Melville House paperback updates Paglen's 2008 hardcover with new patches and research.

Paglen (b. 1974), an American artist and geographer trained at UC Berkeley and the School of the Art Institute of Chicago, makes the classified infrastructure of surveillance and military power visible through photography, sculpture, and investigation. This book followed Torture Taxi and preceded Blank Spots on the Map; he later filmed for Citizenfour, won a MacArthur Fellowship in 2017, and had the survey Sights Unseen at the Smithsonian American Art Museum in 2018.

title: From the Archives of Peter Merlin, Aviation Archaeologist
description:
Trevor Paglen’s From the Archives of Peter Merlin, Aviation Archaeologist is a stark photographic inventory of fifty-nine objects — challenge coins, patches, models, and other classified-program ephemera — drawn from the private archive of Peter Merlin, the country’s foremost historian of secret aircraft.

Merlin, a former NASA archivist, has spent decades collecting flight wreckage, dossiers, and memorabilia from bases such as Area 51 and Edwards Air Force Base and their surrounding crash sites — often the only surviving trace of programs the government never officially acknowledged. Working from Merlin’s conviction that “something always remains,” Paglen photographed fifty-nine pieces, from the atomic age to today’s drone wreckage, in flat, deadpan close-up, paired with his own captions and an essay on secrecy and military symbology. Primary Information published the book — 150 pages, paperback, edited by Miriam Katzeff, designed by David Schoerner.

Trevor Paglen (b. 1974) is an American artist and geographer — PhD in geography, UC Berkeley, 2008 — whose photography, sculpture, and investigative research have examined surveillance and state secrecy since the early 2000s, from long-lens images of black-budget military sites to Mylar satellites launched into orbit. A MacArthur Fellow (2017) and winner of the Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation Prize (2016), he is represented by Pace Gallery, with work held by the Guggenheim, Tate, MoMA, and the Whitney.

description:
The catalogue for Helter Skelter, Fondazione Prada's two-person exhibition setting the American artists Arthur Jafa (b. 1960) and Richard Prince (b. 1949) in dialogue at its Venice venue, Ca' Corner della Regina (9 May – 23 November 2026).

Edited by Nancy Spector with an introduction by Miuccia Prada, it gathers visual essays by both artists, a Jafa–Prince conversation, and Spector's curatorial essay The American Vernacular: Unpolished Truths, alongside commissioned texts by Aria Dean, Ashley James, and Amy Taubin and nine short essays on contemporary American culture by writers including Greil Marcus, Jack Halberstam, Dorian Lynskey, and Beth Coleman, plus plates and the exhibition checklist. The graphic concept is by Peter Saville with design by Graphic Thought Facility; the Venice and Ca' Corner della Regina photographs are by Jöel Tettamanti. The title borrows the Beatles song long entangled with American myths of apocalyptic violence.

Jafa, a cinematographer (Daughters of the Dust) turned artist, won the Golden Lion at the 2019 Venice Biennale and is known for Love Is the Message, the Message Is Death (2016). Prince, a foundational appropriation artist from Untitled (Cowboy) to the Nurse paintings and New Portraits, is already held in depth in the library's collection. A black-and-white reader reprint, Helter Skelter (Dispensa) (Fondazione Prada, 2026), accompanies this catalogue.

title: Afro-Mingei
contributors: Mami Kataoka (Interview); Hirokazu Tokuyama (Essay); Coco Fusco (Essay); Chelsea Foxwell (Essay)
description:
The catalogue for Theaster Gates: Afro-Mingei, the American artist's first solo exhibition in Japan, held at the Mori Art Museum, Tokyo, in 2024.

Published by torch press and edited by the Mori Art Museum, the 272-page, Japanese/English bilingual volume documents Gates's coinage "Afro-Mingei" — a fusion of the Japanese Mingei (folk-craft) movement with African American culture. Trained as a sculptor and urban planner, Gates first travelled to Japan in 2004 to study ceramics in Tokoname; the book threads installation views with interlocking timelines — Tokoname pottery, the Mingei movement, the fictional potter Shoji Yamaguchi, Black American history, and Gates's own biography — alongside his architectural projects, three essays, and an interview with the artist by museum director Mami Kataoka. Texts by Hirokazu Tokuyama, Coco Fusco, and Chelsea Foxwell.

Theaster Gates (b. 1973, Chicago) is a social-practice artist, ceramist, and urban planner whose work spans object-making, performance, and the revival of Chicago's South Side through his Rebuild Foundation and the Stony Island Arts Bank. He has exhibited widely at major international institutions and is represented by Gagosian and White Cube.

title: The Complete Works of Toshiko Okanoue
publisher: Kawade Shobo Shinsha (河出書房新社)
description:
Okanoue Toshiko Zensakuhin (岡上淑子全作品) is the definitive catalogue raisonne of Toshiko Okanoue, the elusive Japanese photomontage artist whose brief, singular body of work reshaped postwar Japanese surrealism.

Published by Kawade Shobo Shinsha in January 2018 as the official catalogue for Okanoue's first major retrospective, "A Long Journey," at the Museum of Art, Kochi, this B5 hardcover assembles all 150 works known to survive: 128 collages and 22 photographs, cut from discarded Allied-occupation-era LIFE and Vogue magazines into uncanny, theatrical tableaux. It includes a complete work list, an inventory of lost pieces, the artist's own writings, a chronology, exhibition history, and an essay by art historian Hiroko Ikegami.

Okanoue (b. 1928, Kochi) studied design at Bunka Gakuin and, over roughly seven years in the 1950s, made collages largely in isolation. Discovered by surrealist critic Shuzo Takiguchi, she exhibited at Takemiya Gallery alongside the VOU poetry circle before marriage led her to set the work aside for four decades. Rediscovered in the late 1990s by historian Ryuichi Kaneko, she now has work held by MoMA, the National Museum of Modern Art Tokyo, and M+ Hong Kong.

title: Los dos amigos
publisher: A&R Press / Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Oaxaca (distributed by Turner Publicaciones)
description:
Los dos amigos documents an eighteen-year collaboration between the Mexican artists Abraham Cruzvillegas and Dr. Lakra, assembled less as a conventional exhibition catalog than as a shared scrapbook of two overlapping creative lives.

Published in 2006 by A&R Press with the Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Oaxaca, the hardcover volume accompanied the artists' first public two-person exhibition, held at MACO in May 2005. Its pages reproduce raw material pulled directly from both artists' source files: magazine clippings, snapshots, posters, fanzines, flyers, found street objects, packaging, correspondence, and personal diaries, tracing an exchange of images built up over two decades rather than presenting finished works in isolation.

Cruzvillegas (b. 1968, Mexico City) works across sculpture and installation under the banner of autoconstrucción, an improvisational building logic drawn from his childhood neighborhood; his work has appeared at Tate Modern, dOCUMENTA (13), and the Venice Biennale. Dr. Lakra (Jerónimo López Ramírez, b. 1972) trained alongside him in Gabriel Orozco's Taller de los Viernes workshop and built a tattoo-derived collage and painting practice mining ethnographic photography and pulp ephemera. The two have kept collaborating as Los dos amigos since, including a mezcal-bottle series shown at kurimanzutto.

title: Black Mirrors
publisher: Galerie du Jour – agnès b./Shelter Press
contributors: agnès b. (Text (Foreword, handwritten letter)); Sinziana Ravini (Text); Peter Sutherland (Text)
description:
Black Mirrors is the first monograph devoted to Julien Langendorff (b. 1982), gathering the Paris-based artist's early collage, drawing, and painting practice into a single fabric-bound artist's book.

Co-published in 2012 by Galerie du Jour – agnès b. (Paris) and Shelter Press (Brussels), the book accompanied Langendorff's solo exhibition Goddess Fuzz Fantasy at agnès b. gallery, New York. Across 64 unpaginated, bilingual French/English pages it gathers pen-and-ink drawings, paper cut-outs of 1970s erotic imagery, and abstract, saturated paintings floating dark, dreamlike forms against black grounds — drawing on gothic and hippie counterculture, Black Sabbath, and spiritism. Bound in thick cardboard wrapped in gray fabric, it includes texts by Langendorff, a handwritten letter from agnès b., Sinziana Ravini, and Peter Sutherland.

Langendorff studied at the École Duperré in Paris and has exhibited in New York, Tokyo, and Berlin since 2005; he met agnès b. in 2009, leading to his representation by Galerie du Jour. He also performs in the doom-psychedelic band Pillars of Fire and records solo as Skate Witches. Black Mirrors captures an early, painting-forward moment that later gave way to the denser, collage-driven work of his subsequent books and zines.
