title: Cutting Edges: Contemporary Collage
editor: Robert Klanten, Hendrik Hellige, James Gallagher
description:
Cutting Edges surveys the early-2010s resurgence of collage as a contemporary art and design practice, gathering the work of dozens of international artists and illustrators who cut, layer, and reassemble found photographs, prints, and ephemera into new compositions.

Published by Gestalten in Berlin in 2011 and edited by Robert Klanten, Hendrik Hellige, and James Gallagher, the 215-page hardcover volume opens with an essay tracing collage's roots in Dada, Surrealism, and Constructivism, the movements that established the technique through artists such as Hannah Höch, John Heartfield, and El Lissitzky, before turning to full-color spreads of contemporary work. Most pieces are made by hand from cut paper and found material rather than digital montage, with several contributors treating the omission of source imagery as deliberately as its addition.

Klanten, Gestalten's founder, has shaped numerous surveys of contemporary visual culture for the publisher, with Hellige co-editing alongside him. James Gallagher, who also wrote the preface, is a New York collage artist trained at the School of Visual Arts; he has since curated international collage exhibitions and, in 2013, founded the art magazine Secret Behavior. Cutting Edges arrived early in a broader wave of surveys cataloguing collage's parallel analog and digital revival.

title: The Age of Collage: Contemporary Collage in Modern Art
description:
The Age of Collage: Contemporary Collage in Modern Art gathers the cut-and-paste practices of dozens of contemporary artists into the first volume of Gestalten's ongoing collage anthology, documenting the medium's resurgence in the early 2010s.

Structured as a survey rather than a monograph, the book opens with a foreword by curator and art historian Silke Krohn tracing collage's lineage from Cubism, Merz, Futurism, Dada, and Surrealism through Pop Art and the combine paintings that followed, before profiling the artists who inherited that vocabulary. The artists collected here mine found photographs, scientific imagery, pop-cultural ephemera, and vintage erotica, favoring an interdisciplinary, cross-media approach that treats destruction and construction as a single gesture.

The volume was edited by Bremen-based artist Dennis Busch (b. 1971) with Gestalten founder Robert Klanten and designer Hendrik Hellige. Busch, who has cut and reassembled vintage imagery since the late 1980s as a self-described image butcher, became the throughline of the series he helped launch: The Age of Collage Vol. 2 followed in 2016, with Vol. 3 continuing the project and expanding its roster of contemporary collage artists.

title: The Age of Collage 2: Contemporary Collage in Modern Art
description:
The second installment in Gestalten's survey of contemporary collage, this anthology gathers work by more than seventy international artists to track how a century-old cut-and-paste technique has expanded into gallery-scale assemblage and digitally assembled composition alike.

Published in 2016, the volume builds on its 2013 predecessor, moving from handmade, analog cut-and-paste toward work produced digitally, and from small-format collage toward large-scale installation and public commission. Artists represented range from established figures such as John Baldessari and Richard Prince to younger practitioners including Lola Dupre, chosen to show collage's reach across fine art, illustration, and design.

The book was edited by Dennis Busch (b. 1971), a Hamburg-based collage artist who originated the Age of Collage project with Gestalten in 2013, together with Gestalten founder Robert Klanten. Busch's own hand-cut, analog practice, built from vintage found imagery, informed the volume's curatorial eye. It is the middle title in a three-part series, preceded by the original Age of Collage (2013, edited by Busch) and followed by The Age of Collage 3 (2020, edited by Klanten and Lincoln Dexter).

title: The Age of Collage 3: Contemporary Collage in Modern Art
description:
The third and concluding volume in Gestalten's Age of Collage series surveys collage as it stood in 2020, tracking a medium defined by juxtaposition, appropriation, and the recombination of found imagery into new, often uncanny, wholes.

Edited by Dennis Busch and Francesca Gavin, the book gathers work by more than sixty international artists, presented as visual portfolios interspersed with short statements on process, materials, and intent. Contributors range from artists working strictly by hand, cutting and pasting found photographs, magazines, and ephemera, to others who build their compositions digitally, and the book treats both as continuous with a single lineage. Published in a full-color, stitch-bound hardcover with a cloth cover, it runs to 320 pages.

Busch, a German collage artist known for hand-cut work built from vintage photography, originated the series with the first volume in 2013 and has edited all three installments; Gavin, a London-based curator and critic and art editor at Twin magazine, joins as co-editor for this closing volume. Together the three books trace collage's shift from a niche craft revival into a widely practiced contemporary medium.

title: One and One Is Four: The Bauhaus Photocollages of Josef Albers
description:
Published by The Museum of Modern Art in 2016, this volume is the first publication to reproduce, in full, the photocollages Josef Albers (1888-1976) made from photographs he shot at the Bauhaus between 1928 and 1932, a body of work unknown until after the artist's death.

Edited by MoMA curator Sarah Hermanson Meister with essays by Elizabeth Otto and Lee Ann Daffner, the book presents roughly seventy collages built from Albers's own snapshots of stadium crowds and scaffolding, regridded into serial arrangements that anticipate the adjacency, repetition, and handcraft-versus-mechanical concerns of his later painting. It accompanied a 2016-17 MoMA installation drawn largely from a 2015 acquisition of ten photocollages, making the Museum's holdings the most extensive outside the Josef and Anni Albers Foundation. 128 pages, 100 illustrations, hardcover.

Albers is best known as a teacher and theorist, at the Bauhaus and later Black Mountain College and Yale, where his treatise Interaction of Color and ongoing Homage to the Square series made him central to postwar geometric abstraction. These photocollages complicate that legacy, showing a more improvisatory, vernacular eye behind the systematic colorist and situating Albers within the Bauhaus's wider culture of experimental photography.

title: John Stezaker: Crossing Over
description:
John Stezaker: Crossing Over gathers a decade of the British collagist's (b. 1949) work with vintage postcards — sixty-five image fragments, incidental details lifted from the edges of found photographs, reprinted at full scale for the first time.

Made between 2005 and 2013 and building on Stezaker's long-running 3rd Person Archive, the fragments trace postcard production from the Victorian era into the postwar period, moving from black-and-white to colour. Stezaker isolates figures at a picture's margin — a passerby, a conversation on a bench — reading these incidental presences as records of time and memory rather than documentary content. Ridinghouse published the 114-page clothbound volume in 2014.

Stezaker studied at the Slade School of Fine Art in the 1960s and taught for decades at Central Saint Martins, Goldsmiths College, and the Royal College of Art, shaping a generation of collage and appropriation artists after him — a pedagogical presence as consequential, in its way, as his own practice of cutting and crossing found pictures. He received the Deutsche Börse Photography Prize in 2012, following his 2011 Whitechapel Gallery retrospective, and is represented by The Approach, London, and Petzel Gallery, New York. The library holds four other Stezaker titles: Nude and Landscape, Silkscreens, One on One, and the Rubell Family Collection volume.

title: John Stezaker: Double Shadow
publisher: Verlag der Buchhandlung Walther König / Ridinghouse
description:
John Stezaker: Double Shadow presents the British collagist's (b. 1949) recent series of paired, doubled silhouettes — an uncanny turn in a five-decade practice built from found photographs.

Cutting figures from 1950s Hollywood publicity portraits and laying the remaining silhouettes as dark shapes against black grounds, Stezaker splits and superimposes two profiles into single hybrid forms — doppelgängers, hermaphrodites, faces that blur masculine and feminine. The seventy-one collages mark what Stezaker has called a rediscovery of 'the pleasures of drawing,' worked entirely in cut paper. Verlag der Buchhandlung Walther König published the 128-page softcover volume with Ridinghouse, following Stezaker's exhibition at The Approach, London (24 February – 26 March 2022), with an essay by Margaret Iversen, 'John Stezaker: Doubles and Shadows.'

The doubling technique extends a method Stezaker has worked for decades: the single, precise cut that joins two found images into one, and the related 3rd Person Archive (1976–present), his ongoing collection of incidental figures clipped from illustrated books. Stezaker came to prominence among the British conceptualists of the 1970s and received the Deutsche Börse Photography Prize in 2012. He is represented by The Approach, London, and Petzel Gallery, New York — the fifth Stezaker title in the library's collection.

title: John Stezaker: Film Still
description:
John Stezaker: Film Still is the first comprehensive survey of the body of work the British collagist (b. 1949) is best known for — collages built from vintage publicity stills clipped from classic-era Hollywood and B-pictures.

Stezaker began cutting into film stills in 1979, a shift away from the text-based conceptualism of his earlier work, and the series has run continuously since. The 144-page volume traces its evolution: an early reliance on Hitchcock's American-period stills gives way to the anonymous mass of low-budget 1940s and early 1950s studio product, as Stezaker's excisions and superimpositions turn found publicity photography into images of estrangement and doubling. Ridinghouse published the softcover survey in 2011 with a critical essay by David Campany and a recorded conversation between Campany and the artist.

The library's other Stezaker catalog, Nude and Landscape, reads the artist against art-historical tradition specifically to move away from 'the cinematic imagery his found-image work is best known for' — this volume returns directly to that imagery, the source material Stezaker has mined longest. He came to prominence among the British conceptualists of the 1970s and received the Deutsche Börse Photography Prize in 2012, following his 2011 Whitechapel Gallery retrospective. He is represented by The Approach, London, and Petzel Gallery, New York.

title: John Stezaker: Lost World
contributors: Geoffrey Batchen (Essay); David Campany (Essay); Robert Leonard (Essay)
description:
John Stezaker: Lost World catalogs a touring survey of the British collagist's (b. 1949) work, built on his account of collage as 'a yearning for a lost world' — images from an archive of out-of-date film stills, actor headshots, and postcards that have lost their immediate relationship to the world they depicted.

Alongside the collages, the book documents Stezaker's found-object sculptures — antique mannequin hands arranged as a repertoire of gestures — and Crowd, a film work presenting hundreds of film-still crowd scenes for a single frame each. Ridinghouse published the 88-page softcover catalog in 2017 with essays by Geoffrey Batchen, David Campany, and curator Robert Leonard, for the exhibition Leonard organized at City Gallery Wellington (26 August – 19 November 2017), which toured to the Govett-Brewster Art Gallery, New Plymouth; Christchurch Art Gallery; and the Centre for Contemporary Photography, Melbourne, through late 2018.

The tour across four New Zealand and Australian venues reflects how far Stezaker's reputation now extends beyond Britain: his work sits in the collections of MoMA, Tate, and the Art Gallery of New South Wales. He came to prominence among the British conceptualists of the 1970s and received the Deutsche Börse Photography Prize in 2012, following his 2011 Whitechapel Gallery retrospective. He is represented by The Approach, London, and Petzel Gallery, New York — the library's fifth Stezaker title.

title: John Stezaker
publisher: Ridinghouse, in association with Whitechapel Gallery, Mudam Luxembourg, and Mildred Lane Kemper Art Museum
contributors: Dawn Ades (Essay); Michael Bracewell (Essay); Daniel F. Herrmann (Interview); Christophe Gallois (Interview)
description:
John Stezaker is the largest monographic survey yet published on the British collagist (b. 1949), the catalog for his 2011 Whitechapel Gallery retrospective — the exhibition that established Stezaker, after four decades of work, as a defining figure in photographic appropriation.

The 220-page volume gathers found images, collages, and image fragments made from the 1970s onward, including a selection from The 3rd Person Archive, Stezaker's ongoing collection of incidental figures clipped from illustrated books, in over 120 illustrations. Essays by Dawn Ades and Michael Bracewell place the work in art-historical context, alongside a conversation between Stezaker and curators Daniel F. Herrmann and Christophe Gallois. Ridinghouse published the softcover volume with Whitechapel Gallery, Mudam Luxembourg, and the Mildred Lane Kemper Art Museum, which hosted the exhibition on its tour.

The Whitechapel retrospective this catalog accompanies proved a turning point in Stezaker's reception: it led directly to his winning the Deutsche Börse Photography Prize in 2012, a notable choice for an artist who has never taken a photograph. He is represented by The Approach, London, and Petzel Gallery, New York. This is the definitive survey among the library's Stezaker holdings, alongside Nude and Landscape, Silkscreens, One on One, the Rubell Family Collection volume, and the batch added with it: Crossing Over, Double Shadow, Film Still, and Lost World.

title: When I Was a Boy
description:
When I Was a Boy (2018) is Katrien De Blauwer's contribution to Libraryman's Seasons Series, a compact monograph built from found photographs the Belgian artist (b. 1969) cuts, layers, and reassembles into image without ever touching a camera.

The book gathers 27 color plates drawn from De Blauwer's practice of collecting vintage magazine and studio photography, then cutting each image down to a single ambiguous gesture — a shoulder, a collar, a half-obscured face — so that presence and erasure sit on the same page. Bound as a color offset hardcover with linen thread binding, a brown headband, and white foil-stamped cover typography, the 32-page volume was released in an edition of 500, with a signed 25-copy special edition in a screenprinted slipcase. It was shortlisted for the Author Book Award at Les Rencontres d'Arles in 2018.

De Blauwer, who studied painting in Ghent before abandoning fashion studies at Antwerp's Royal Academy, calls herself a "photographer without a camera": her collages work by subtraction and accumulation, the cut standing in for the frame. She is represented by Galerie Les Filles du Calvaire in Paris and Gallery Fifty One in Antwerp, and shows regularly at Paris Photo and Art Brussels; When I Was a Boy inaugurated a run of Libraryman monographs that continued with Why I Hate Cars (2019) and You Could at Least Pretend to Like Yellow (2020).
tags: Collage, Photography, Artist Books, Belgian Art, Contemporary Art

title: Why I Hate Cars
description:
Why I Hate Cars (2019) follows Katrien De Blauwer's When I Was a Boy with a darker, more painterly turn: the Belgian artist begins layering paint and crayon directly over her cut photographic fragments, adding a second register of mark-making to a practice she still calls "photography without a camera."

The 72-page hardcover gathers 64 color plates built from collected magazine and newspaper imagery — car interiors, rear windows, half-visible passengers — overpainted in flat bands of red and black that block as much as they reveal. An excerpt from the artist's notebooks runs through the volume, and the book accompanied De Blauwer's 2019 Paris exhibition "Love me Tender" at Galerie Les Filles du Calvaire. Libraryman printed it in an edition of 1,000, offset and linen thread bound with a red headband and tipped-in cover images, alongside a 50-copy special edition with a hand-drawn signed print.

De Blauwer (b. 1969, Ronse) works by cutting rather than combining, treating the edge of the photograph as the meaningful gesture rather than the picture inside it. Why I Hate Cars sits at the midpoint of her ongoing Libraryman series, between the quieter When I Was a Boy and the more chromatic You Could at Least Pretend to Like Yellow, from a period in which her collages moved from art-fair presentations at Paris Photo and Art Brussels into gallery solo shows at Les Filles du Calvaire and Gallery Fifty One.

title: You Could at Least Pretend to Like Yellow
description:
You Could at Least Pretend to Like Yellow (2020) is the eighth book by Belgian collage artist Katrien De Blauwer, and the first in her Libraryman series to organize an entire monograph around a single color rather than a single subject.

De Blauwer built the book around a chance discovery: a companion volume to Vilgot Sjöman's 1967 film I Am Curious (Yellow), found in an antique shop before she had seen the film itself — "pretending to like yellow" while she waited. The 40-page hardcover reproduces 40 works in color, each printed at its actual individual size and paired, unusually, with the verso of the cut photograph as well as its front, giving equal weight to the residue of the source image and the collage made from it. Libraryman produced it as a linen-thread-bound, color offset hardcover with a yellow headband and printed endpapers, in an edition of 450 with 250 signed copies.

The book extends what Libraryman calls De Blauwer's practice of "cut" rather than collage — recovering discarded photographs and giving them a second, private narrative rather than fusing them into new composite scenes. Since her first collage books in the early 1990s, De Blauwer has shown at Paris Photo and Art Brussels and is represented by Galerie Les Filles du Calvaire, Gallery Fifty One, and Rosegallery; Yellow followed Why I Hate Cars and When I Was a Boy as the third of her Libraryman monographs built around memory by accumulation rather than subtraction.

title: Cosmic Surgery
description:
Cosmic Surgery (2016) imagines cosmetic surgery rerouted through geometry: British-based photographer Alma Haser (b. 1989) folds her own portrait sitters into faceted origami masks built from photographs of their own features, so that eyes, lips, and cheekbones multiply across the folded planes of a paper polyhedron fixed to the face.

The self-published hardcover collects portraits from a project Haser began in 2013, photographing each sitter twice — once straight, once concealed beneath a folded paper construction printed with details from the same shoot — so that cubist multiplication stands in for the "cosmetic" transformation the title puns on (Haser, who is dyslexic, coined it by misspeaking "cosmetic surgery"). This second edition, funded through a 2016 Kickstarter and designed by Emily Macaulay of Stanley/Barker, runs 60 pages plus inserted booklets of speculative pseudo-medical text by science writer Piers Bizony describing the procedure's features and benefits; the hardcover is foil-embossed on cover, spine, and back, in a signed edition of 600.

Haser studied photography at Nottingham Trent University, where she also took up origami, graduating in 2010; she works across analogue paper-folding, collage, and rephotography to push flat portraiture toward sculpture. Cosmic Surgery won the Magenta Foundation's Bright Spark Award and remains her best-known monograph, anchoring a body of work that continued with the twin-portrait jigsaws of Within 15 Minutes and the paper-and-plant hybrids of her ongoing Plant series.

title: Linder
description:
Published by Ridinghouse in 2015, Linder is the most comprehensive printed survey to date of work by the British artist Linder (b. Linder Sterling, 1954, Liverpool), gathering four decades of photomontage that splice advertising, pornography, and domestic imagery into a sustained feminist critique of gender and consumer culture.

The volume gathers over 240 works, interweaving Linder's recurring series rather than a single chronology. Die-cut pages and paper-stock shifts, developed with the artist's input, echo the images' own collage logic. 255 illustrations accompany a conversation between Linder and the art historian Dawn Adès, situating her work within photomontage's wider history, from Dada through punk-era graphic design.

Linder emerged from Manchester's punk scene, designing the Buzzcocks' "Orgasm Addict" sleeve (1977) and, with Morrissey, the fanzine The Secret Public. Her signature technique — fusing fashion imagery, pornography, and domestic appliances — critiques manufactured femininity, later extended into performance as frontwoman of Ludus. Surveys at Tate St Ives, the Hepworth Wakefield, MoMA PS1, and the Musée d'Art Moderne de Paris affirm her place as a central figure in feminist photomontage.

description:
Linderism is the catalogue for the first UK museum survey of the British artist Linder (b. 1954), published by Kettle's Yard, University of Cambridge, and Koenig Books to accompany her 2020 Cambridge retrospective.

The volume reproduces work spanning Linder's career, from the punk-era photomontages she began exhibiting in Manchester fanzines through her later photographic and performance work, alongside working drawings and research images. Four essays, by James Boaden, Alyce Mahon, Amy Tobin and Sarah Victoria Turner, address her methods of image-making and her turn toward spirituality and the occult, edited by Amy Tobin with Alina Khakoo. Curated by Amy Tobin, the exhibition was the first UK survey to trace the full breadth of Linder's practice, positioning her within a longer history of British feminist art rather than only the post-punk milieu that first brought her attention. It drew on Linder's decades-long collaboration with Morrissey, her design commissions for fashion houses including Richard Nicoll, and new site-specific performances staged across Kettle's Yard, reassessing her legacy within British feminist art history.

title: Linder: Femme/Objet
contributors: Fabrice Hergott (Essay); Emmanuelle de l'Ecotais (Curator / Essay); Morrissey (Interview)
description:
Linder: Femme/Objet is the catalogue for the first full retrospective of the British artist Linder (Linder Sterling, b. 1954), staged by the Musée d'Art Moderne de la Ville de Paris / ARC in 2013 and tracing four decades of photomontage.

Structured like a magazine, the 112-page volume accompanies an exhibition of nearly 200 works — photographs, photomontages, light boxes, costumes, and performance documentation — curated by Emmanuelle de l'Ecotais and shown at the ARC from 1 February to 21 April 2013. Co-published by Paris Musées and Walther König, it reproduces roughly eighty works alongside essays by museum director Fabrice Hergott and de l'Ecotais, plus an interview between Linder and Morrissey.

Linder's photomontage — splicing pornography, fashion advertising, and appliance catalogues into one image — extends a lineage of political collage running through John Heartfield and, most directly, Hannah Höch's Weimar-era critiques of the “New Woman.” The title Femme/Objet names that critique: cut faces and catalogue bodies stage the female figure as commodity, carrying Dada and Surrealist concerns into a punk and post-punk register. The retrospective marked a major European institutional endorsement of that work; Linder continues to exhibit internationally, represented by Modern Art, London.

title: John Heartfield: Fotografie plus Dynamit
description:
John Heartfield: Fotografie plus Dynamit is the catalog for a major Akademie der Künste retrospective on John Heartfield (1891-1968), the Berlin Dada artist who turned photomontage into a weapon against fascism and war.

Co-published by the Akademie der Künste and Hirmer Verlag and edited by Angela Lammert, Anna Schultz, and Rosa von der Schulenburg, the 311-page volume draws on the Academy's own Heartfield Archive to survey his career across 250 color reproductions, from his Berlin Dada beginnings through his AIZ covers attacking Hitler and the Nazi regime to his postwar design work in East Germany. The exhibition opened at the Akademie der Künste in March 2020 before traveling to Museum de Fundatie in Zwolle and the Royal Academy of Arts in London.

Heartfield co-founded Berlin Dada with George Grosz and his brother, the writer Wieland Herzfelde, pairing found photographs with blunt captions to devastating satirical effect. His AIZ covers of the 1930s remain touchstones of anti-fascist visual culture and a foundational reference for later photomontage and collage artists working in political protest.

title: Negative Space
description:
Negative Space is a hand-bound artist's book by the San Francisco collage artist Matt Borruso, assembling found imagery into a strange, self-contained world of swamp creatures, mushroom-crowned cavemen, and exoskeletal beings.

Working from stacks of found photographs, magazines, and printed ephemera, Borruso collages source images into scenes of ritual and mutation, building a spectral, paranormal realm of evolutionary defects and hybrid bodies. Published under the artist's own imprint, Visible Publications, San Francisco, in a hand-bound edition of 50 hardcover copies with a one-color hand-screened cover and hand-sewn binding; a softcover second edition of 100 followed in 2017. The book runs 44 pages in full color, at 10.25 x 7.5 inches (26 x 19 cm).

Borruso received his MFA from Yale University (2004) and BFA from the San Francisco Art Institute (2002), and has shown solo at Steven Wolf Fine Arts, 2nd Floor Projects, and Et al. in San Francisco, and Black Ball Projects in Brooklyn. Under Visible Publications, he has made collage-based artist's books since 2010 — including IMAGE File and Cave Life — held in the library collections of MoMA, the Whitney Museum, SFMOMA, and the International Center of Photography.

title: DATA
description:
DATA is a hand-screened artist's book by the San Francisco collage artist Matt Borruso, pairing flat bands of color with high-contrast, halftone-screened photographs to build an ambiguous, quasi-mechanical body language out of appropriated imagery.

Self-published in 2019 under Borruso's own imprint, Visible Publications, the book runs 56 pages in black and white, bound in a two-color, hand-screened softcover printed in an edition of 60 — each copy pulled in one of two colorways, orange or pink, over a shared cover image of a gloved hand gripping a length of pipe. Borruso builds each spread from cropped, rescreened photographs and ephemera, coarsening found pictures into heavy halftone dots until figures dissolve into pattern and texture. Hand-sewn binding and hand-screening tie the book to the small-run, DIY tradition of West Coast zine and print culture.

Borruso received his MFA from Yale (2004) and BFA from the San Francisco Art Institute (2002), and has shown solo at Steven Wolf Fine Arts, Et al., and Black Ball Projects. Since founding Visible Publications in 2010, he has released a steady run of collage-based artist's books — including Negative Space and Cave Life — held in the library collections of MoMA, the Whitney Museum, SFMOMA, and the ICP; DATA sits within that same body of self-published work.

title: Frank Peter John Dick
description:
Frank Peter John Dick (2011) is the debut publication of American artist K8 Hardy, collecting photo collages she assembled privately, over several years, from magazines, advertisements, and found photographs as working research for her performance and photographic practice.

The book reproduces the collages largely as made: cut-and-glued fragments of fashion editorials, newsprint headlines, darkroom test strips, and junk-store snapshots, layered into studies of representation, style, and queer identity. Its cover assembles broken male first names — Frank, Peter, John, Richard, Steve, Gary, Robert — literalizing the title as found-text collage. Never made for exhibition, the material became a book only after studio visitors urged Hardy to publish it; Capricious released it as 52 full-color, perfect-bound pages, with an essay by Eileen Myles and endnotes by the artist identifying her sources.

Hardy (b. 1977, Fort Worth, Texas) co-founded the queer feminist collective and journal LTTR in 2002 and holds an MFA from Bard College (2008). This collage practice underlies the photography, sculpture, and performance for which she is better known, including the Position Series photographs and her 2012 Whitney Biennial runway performance; her work is held in the Whitney, Guggenheim, and MoMA collections, and she is represented by Reena Spaulings Fine Art.

title: Stereosophic Conjunctions
editor: Frank van der Stok and Paul Bogaers
description:
Stereosophic Conjunctions (2016) gathers twenty-seven photographic pairings by Dutch artist Paul Bogaers, in which found snapshots, postcards, and magazine clippings collide with his own photographs into surreal, associative collisions.

Printed originally as black-and-white gelatin silver prints and reproduced here in duotone, the pairings set unrelated images — an amateur snapshot, a postcard, a torn magazine page — against each other in what Bogaers calls ‘gedachtenfotografie,’ or thought-photography: a medium built to describe the visible world turned toward picturing an inner one. The title puns on stereoscopy, echoed by the paired viewfinders on its orange cover. Published 2016 by Timmer Art Books, an imprint of Lecturis (Eindhoven), as a 48-page, cahier-stitched softcover designed by Rob van Hoesel and edited by Frank van der Stok and the artist.

Paul Bogaers (b. 1961, Tilburg) has worked since the 1980s across photography, collage, and sculptural assemblage, drawing on a growing archive of found and self-made images recombined into associative sequences rather than documentary series. Stereosophic Conjunctions isolates that collecting-and-pairing method, also central to Les Vacances de M. Rorschach, as a subject on its own.

title: Man Ray
description:
This TASCHEN monograph surveys Man Ray (1890–1976), the American-born photographer, painter, and filmmaker whose rayographs, solarizations, and Surrealist portraits redefined what a camera could do.

Issued in TASCHEN's compact Icons format, the 192-page hardcover moves from Man Ray's early New York experiments through his central Paris years, pairing reproductions with text by photography curator Katherine Ware and editorial direction by Manfred Heiting. It surveys his still lifes, fashion work, portraiture, and nude studies alongside the camera-less "rayographs" and solarized prints he pioneered, reproducing signature images including Noire et blanche and Le Violon d’Ingres.

Born Emmanuel Radnitzky in Philadelphia, Man Ray moved to Paris in 1921 and became a central figure of Dada and Surrealism, working across painting, film, sculpture, and object-making as fluently as photography, and photographing the Parisian avant-garde—Duchamp, Breton, Kiki de Montparnasse—along the way. TASCHEN has kept a Man Ray title in print in several forms since 2000; this compact edition is the publisher’s current standard survey of his work.

title: XAMAX
description:
XAMAX is an artist's book by the Swiss artist Fabian Boschung (b. 1983) that borrows its title and graphic identity, bold red-and-black stripes, from Neuchâtel Xamax, the football club of the city where he lives and works, turning a local sporting emblem into a study in pattern and appropriation.

Published in 2017 by TSAR Éditions in Vevey, Switzerland, the 48-page paperback carries the club's stripe motif and wordmark across its cover in place of any imagery of the team, treating the crest and colorway as a found visual system to be isolated, repeated, and re-staged as abstract composition, characteristic of Boschung's broader practice of appropriating forms and iconography from official emblems and vernacular material alike.

Boschung trained in graphic design in La Chaux-de-Fonds before studying visual art at HEAD Genève. He works across sculpture, painting, neon, and photography, has exhibited at CAN Centre d'art Neuchâtel and elsewhere since 2010, and is represented by Galerie Lange + Pult in Zurich. Xamax is the second of his two artist's books, following Feeling (2013), his first monograph, and shares its deadpan, design-forward approach to found imagery.

title: FIN?
description:
FIN? is a zine of killed, rejected, and forgotten studio work by the Manchester design duo DR.ME (Ryan Doyle and Mark Edwards), a running archive of the ideas that didn't survive the brief.

Launched as a monthly, free-to-download PDF — a "Print It Yourself" release built from client and personal-project offcuts that would otherwise sit unused in plan chests and hard drives — FIN? gathered its best material every six months into a printed compilation. Across its run DR.ME produced 29 P.I.Y. digital issues and 5 printed issues, some 540 artworks in total, before the studio stopped making new issues in 2019. The library holds that 2019 printed issue, by the duo's own account the series' final year. Its cover is built from the same raw collage vocabulary — cut barcodes, crossed-out file names, sticker-sheet fragments — that runs through the interior pages.

DR.ME is the studio name of Ryan Doyle and Mark Edwards, a Manchester, UK design partnership working across branding, illustration, and collage-driven art direction. FIN? sits outside that commercial practice: a self-published side project the pair used to keep rejected work in circulation and to push themselves toward constantly making something new.

title: The Luxury of Rigor
description:
The Luxury of Rigor (2013) is an early zine from Matt Borruso's San Francisco imprint Visible Publications, built entirely from appropriated photography run through screen-printed color and half-tone texture.

Printed in full color across 54 softcover pages in an open edition, the book cuts between glossy shelter-magazine interiors, close-up geological studies of salt and mineral crystal, a horror-film still, and the printer's own registration bars and color-swatch keys - treating the tools of commercial reproduction as material for the collage itself. The title's dry pairing of "luxury" and "rigor" frames the method: found images of aspirational excess are handled with the same deadpan, process-driven attention as the production marks that interrupt them.

Borruso has run Visible Publications since 2010, self-publishing close to twenty small-run, hand-assembled books that mine found imagery, screen printing, and appropriation. Hudson Street Library also holds his Negative Space (2010), DATA (2019), and Wax House of Wax (2016), all produced under the same imprint.

title: Lounge of Psychedelia
description:
Lounge of Psychedelia (2020) is a large-format art book by the Tokyo graphic artist Keiji Ito (b. 1958), built around an invented record shop of the same name that anchors his collage-driven, psychedelic visual world.

Published by G/P+abp as part of the Fuji Xerox-supported NEOTOKYOZINE (NTZ) series, the softcover volume unfolds Ito's fictional "Lounge of Psychedelia Records" - a shop perched beneath a smoking volcano, its porch lined with lounge chairs and houseplants - through the dense, hand-drawn collage of pattern, line, and pop iconography that runs through both his commercial and gallery work. At 31.8 x 23.6 cm, the book gives that imagery room to read as much like poster art as illustration.

Ito founded the Tokyo studio UFG (Unidentified Flying Graphics) and teaches at Kyoto University of the Arts. His art direction and collage-based illustration run through the 2005 Aichi Expo's official poster, NHK title sequences, and campaigns for Coca-Cola, SoftBank, and Converse (Tokyo ADC Award, 2001), alongside a 1999 New York ADC Gold Medal and CD-jacket work for Japanese musicians including Bonnie Pink and Orange Pekoe.

title: Targets
description:
A pointed artist's book by the New York artist Anne Doran, Targets holds two vocabularies of the aimed-at body in a single frame: vintage pornography stills seamlessly collaged with the human-silhouette practice targets of the shooting range.

Across forty-eight digitally printed color pages, the black target silhouettes — their scoring numbers and manufacturer's imprint left legible — are cut into and overlaid with anonymous nudes, so that zones of desire and zones of aim coincide. Published in New York by Ratstar Press in 2018 as a perfect-bound paperback, the book presents one collage per page, plate-style, and examines, in the publisher's phrasing, how the body can be a target for action and a catalyst for power.

Doran's appropriation-based photo-collage practice dates to New York in the mid-1980s; her Photo-works (1985–1991), revisited in a later gallery survey, drew on the same found-image economy of advertising, pornography, and print ephemera that Targets distills to its starkest pairing.

notes: The library holds two copies.
